## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Rathalaṭṭhijātaka* (Ja 332) is a canonical Jātaka tale translated in English as *The Chariot-Whip* [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered the tale while residing at Jetavana concerning the royal priest (*purohita*) of the king of Kosala [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. While driving his chariot along a narrow road to an estate village, the enraged chaplain shouted at a caravan to clear out of his way and hurled his goad-stick (*patodalaṭṭhi*) at the foremost cart driver [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].
In the story of the past, a king judged a legal dispute without examining both sides, prompting his wise councillor—the Bodhisatta—to reprove him [Ānandajoti 2010]. The opening verse addresses deeds done amiss and condemns those whose conduct is not good, observing that a lazy layperson who pursues sensual pleasures is not good (*Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu*) [Ānandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. Upon hearing the Bodhisatta's admonition, the king re-adjudicated the dispute righteousiy according to Dhamma, establishing that the fault lay with the brahmin [Fausböll 1883]. In the identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the royal councillor as himself and the chaplain as the past brahmin [Fausböll 1883].
Curated parallels in non-Pali collections are not attested on SuttaCentral, though four modern translations into four languages are recorded [SuttaCentral]. Machine text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus identifies five Pali-internal matches across two commentary texts: the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest alignment §§1.1–5.1) and the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest alignment §§3.1–4.4) [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language matches meeting the reporting threshold were identified [DharmaNexus].
